title: Al-Baqarah
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
Al-Baqarah is the longest surah of the Qur'an, two hundred and eighty-six verses that run from the opening letters "Alif-Lãm-Mĩm" to the closing prayer "do not burden us with more than we can bear". It was the first long surah to come down after the Prophet ﷺ moved to Madinah, and it reads like the charter of the new community: who believes and who only pretends to, what happened to the nations who received scripture before, why the Kaʿbah is the direction of prayer, and how a Muslim fasts, fights, marries, divorces, lends, gives and dies. Khālid ibn Maʿdān called it the Fusṭāṭ of the Qur'an, its great tent, and some scholars said it holds a thousand reports, a thousand commands and a thousand prohibitions.

The Prophet ﷺ gave it the highest praise he gave any surah. He said that Shayṭān does not enter a house where it is recited, that it and Āl ʿImrān will come on the Day of Resurrection as two clouds shading the people who lived by them, and that learning it is a blessing while neglecting it is a sorrow. His Companions called out its name as a battle cry at Ḥunayn and at al-Yamāmah. Everything in this introduction about its standing comes from those reports.

### Where and when it was revealed

There is no disagreement that the whole of Al-Baqarah was revealed in Madinah. Ibn ʿAbbās said so, in the report of Ibn Jurayj from ʿAṭāʾ, and so did ʿAbdullāh ibn az-Zubayr, in the report of Khaṣīf from Mujāhid, and the leading scholars of tafsīr agree. It was among the first surahs revealed there, yet it also holds the last verse of the Qur'an to come down: "Be mindful of the Day when you will ˹all˺ be returned to Allah" (2:281). The verses on usury, near the end of the surah, were also among the very last to be revealed, so the surah spans the whole Madinan period.

Those who counted its text gave two hundred and eighty-seven verses by their way of counting, six thousand two hundred and twenty-one words and twenty-five thousand five hundred letters. In the numbering used here it has two hundred and eighty-six verses.

### What its names mean

- **Al-Baqarah**, "The Cow", after the story in verses 67 to 74 of the cow the Children of Israel were told to sacrifice and questioned about until the simple command had become almost impossible.
- **Fusṭāṭ al-Qur'an**, "the tent of the Qur'an", the name Khālid ibn Maʿdān used, because so much of the religion is housed in it.
- **The hump of the Qur'an.** Sahl ibn Saʿd reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that everything has a hump, its high point, and the hump of the Qur'an is Al-Baqarah. The report was collected by Abū al-Qāsim aṭ-Ṭabarānī, by Abū Ḥātim Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and by Ibn Mardawayh.

### Its virtues

Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not turn your houses into graves. Shayṭān does not enter the house in which Sūrat Al-Baqarah is recited." It is recorded by Aḥmad, Muslim, at-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ, and an-Nasāʾī. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said that Shayṭān runs from a house in which Al-Baqarah is heard, a report an-Nasāʾī has in his work on the day and the night and al-Ḥākim in his Mustadrak, where he called its chain authentic although the two Ṣaḥīḥs did not include it. Ad-Dārimī recorded Ibn Masʿūd's blunter version, that Shayṭān leaves the house where it is recited and breaks wind as he goes.

Ad-Dārimī also recorded, through ash-Shaʿbī, Ibn Masʿūd's advice on ten verses: whoever recites ten verses of Al-Baqarah in a night, four from its beginning, the Verse of the Throne (255) with the two verses after it (256 and 257), and its last three verses, Shayṭān will not enter his house that night. Another narration adds that Shayṭān will not come near him or his family, nothing he dislikes will touch him, and if these verses are recited over a man whose mind has gone, they will rouse him.

In the hadith of Sahl ibn Saʿd about the hump of the Qur'an, the Prophet ﷺ added that whoever recites Al-Baqarah in his house at night, Shayṭān will not enter it for three nights, and whoever recites it in his house by day, Shayṭān will not enter it for three days.

Abū Hurayrah also told of an expedition the Prophet ﷺ sent out. He asked each man what he had memorized of the Qur'an and came to one of the youngest, who said he knew such and such surahs and Al-Baqarah. The Prophet ﷺ asked, "You have memorized Sūrat Al-Baqarah?" and when the young man said yes, he said, "Then you are their commander." One of the leading men admitted that he had never learned Al-Baqarah for fear that he would not live up to it. The Prophet ﷺ answered with a comparison: learn the Qur'an and recite it, for the one who learns it, recites it and acts on it is like a bag full of musk whose scent fills the air, while the one who learns it and then sleeps with it in his memory is like a bag of musk tied shut. At-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah recorded it. At-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan and also has it in a mursal form.

Al-Bukhārī recorded what happened to Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr one night. He was reciting Al-Baqarah with his horse tied beside him. The horse grew restless. When he stopped, it stood still, and when he began again, it moved about again, and this happened more than once. His son Yaḥyā was lying near the horse, and Usayd feared it would trample the boy. When he went to move him and looked up, he saw something like a cloud filled with lights like lamps. In the morning he told the Prophet ﷺ, who asked whether he knew what it was, and then told him: those were the angels, who had drawn near to his voice, and had he gone on reading, people would have seen them when morning came, for they would not have been hidden from their eyes. Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām also related it in his book on the virtues of the Qur'an.

### Al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān, the two lights

Buraydah said that he was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ when he heard him say, "Learn Sūrat Al-Baqarah, for in learning it there is blessing, in leaving it there is sorrow, and the sorceresses cannot memorize it." After a silence the Prophet ﷺ went on: learn Al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān, for they are two lights that will shade their people on the Day of Resurrection like two clouds, two canopies of shade or two flocks of birds in flight. He then described how the Qur'an meets its companion when his grave is opened, in the form of a pale-faced man who asks, "Do you know me?" When the man says he does not, the Qur'an says that it is his companion who made him thirsty in the heat and kept him awake at night, and that while every merchant has his trade, today he stands above all trade. Kingship is placed in his right hand and eternal life in his left, a crown of honour is set on his head, and his parents are dressed in two garments that the people of this world could never afford. When they ask why, they are told: because your son carried the Qur'an. Then he is told to read and ascend through the levels of Paradise, rising as long as he recites, whether slowly or quickly. Aḥmad recorded this through ʿAbdullāh ibn Buraydah from his father. Ibn Mājah recorded part of it from Bishr ibn al-Muhājir, with a chain that is ḥasan by Muslim's standard.

Abū Umāmah al-Bāhilī heard the Prophet ﷺ say that the Qur'an will intercede for its people on the Day of Resurrection, and that the two lights, Al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān, will come as two clouds, two shades or two flocks of birds and plead for the people who kept them. He added the words about blessing and sorrow and the sorceresses. Aḥmad recorded it, and Muslim has it in his Book of Prayer. An-Nawwās ibn Samʿān reported that the Qur'an and the people who lived by it will be brought forward on that Day with Al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān at their head, and that the Prophet ﷺ gave three likenesses for the two surahs which he never forgot: two clouds, two dark shades, or two lines of birds arguing for their people. Aḥmad and Muslim recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan gharīb.

### The surah in battle, and at the Jamrah

Ibn Mardawayh recorded, through Shuʿbah from ʿAqīl ibn Ṭalḥah from ʿUtbah ibn Marthad, that the Prophet ﷺ once saw his Companions were not in the front lines and called, "O Companions of Sūrat Al-Baqarah!" This is thought to have happened at Ḥunayn, when the Companions fell back. The Prophet ﷺ told his uncle al-ʿAbbās to shout, "O Companions of the tree!", the men who had given the pledge of ar-Riḍwān under the tree, and in another narration al-ʿAbbās cried, "O Companions of Sūrat Al-Baqarah!", and they came back from every side. Later, at the battle of al-Yamāmah against the army of Musaylimah the Liar, the Companions first gave ground before his huge numbers, and the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār rallied one another with the cry "O people of Sūrat Al-Baqarah!" until Allah gave them victory.

The two Ṣaḥīḥs also record Ibn Masʿūd at the pilgrimage, standing with the Kaʿbah on his left and Minā on his right, throwing seven pebbles and saying that this is how the one to whom Sūrat Al-Baqarah was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ, performed the rite. The surah's name had become a way of naming the Prophet ﷺ himself.

### What the surah covers

The surah opens with three of the fourteen separate letters that begin twenty-nine surahs of the Qur'an, and with the statement that this Book is beyond doubt and guides the mindful (verses 1 and 2). It then draws three portraits: the believers (3 to 5), the disbelievers (6 and 7) and, at greatest length, the hypocrites, with two parables about them (8 to 20). From there it calls all people to worship the One who made them, challenges doubters to produce a single surah like it, promises Paradise to those who believe and do good, explains why Allah uses parables, and points to His power in creation (21 to 29).

The story of Ādam follows: his creation as a vicegerent, the angels' question, the names he was taught, Iblīs's refusal, the garden, the slip and the forgiveness (30 to 39). Then comes the longest address in the Qur'an to the Children of Israel (40 to 123): the covenant and its favours, deliverance from Firʿawn, the calf, the demand to see Allah, the manna and the quails, the twelve springs, the Sabbath-breakers, the story of the cow that gives the surah its name, the scholars who sold the truth, the claim that the Fire would touch them only for a few days, the prophets they rejected, Jibrīl, the magic of Bābil, and the claims about Paradise and about Allah having a son.

Ibrāhīm is next (124 to 141): his test, the building of the Kaʿbah with Ismāʿīl, his prayers for Makkah and for a messenger from his descendants, and his religion as the common faith of all the prophets. The change of the direction of prayer from Jerusalem to the Kaʿbah is set out and defended (142 to 152), followed by patience under trial, the walk between Ṣafā and Marwah, the sin of hiding guidance, Allah's oneness and His signs, lawful and forbidden food, and the famous definition of righteousness in verse 177 (153 to 177).

The law then takes over (178 to 242): retaliation for murder, bequests, the fast of Ramaḍān and its nights, fighting and its limits, Ḥajj and ʿUmrah, charity, the sacred months, wine and gambling, orphans, marriage to idolaters, menstruation, oaths, divorce and the waiting period, nursing, provision for widows, and the guarding of prayers. A story breaks the sequence of rulings: the Israelites who asked for a king, Ṭālūt, the ark, the river and Dāwūd's defeat of Jālūt (243 to 253).

The surah closes with its highest passages (254 to 286): the call to spend before the Day comes, the Verse of the Throne, the statement that there is no compulsion in religion, three stories of faith and resurrection (Ibrāhīm and the king, the man who passed a ruined town, and the four birds), a long section on charity and its manners, the condemnation of usury, mercy toward debtors, the longest verse in the Qur'an on recording debts, Allah's ownership of all that is in the heavens and the earth, the declaration of faith of the Messenger and the believers, and the prayer that ends it.

### In short

- Al-Baqarah is the longest surah, revealed entirely in Madinah, among the first there and holding the last verse of the Qur'an to be revealed (2:281).
- The Prophet ﷺ said Shayṭān does not enter a house where it is recited, that it is the hump of the Qur'an, and that it and Āl ʿImrān are two lights that will shade their people on the Day of Resurrection.
- Learning it brings blessing, leaving it brings sorrow, and its name served the Companions as a battle cry at Ḥunayn and al-Yamāmah.
- It moves from the three kinds of people, through Ādam, the Children of Israel and Ibrāhīm, to the Qiblah, the law of the community, and the Verse of the Throne, and ends with a prayer.

1.text:
The longest surah of the Qur'an opens with three letters of the alphabet, "Alif-Lãm-Mĩm", read one by one by their names. They are not a word and they are not a sentence. Twenty-nine surahs begin in this way, and from the time of the Companions onward the question of what these letters mean has been answered with a careful mixture of reverence and restraint: Allah knows what He meant by them, the scholars have offered readings, and everyone agrees that they were not sent down for nothing.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Alif-Lãm-Mĩm"** is three letters, the equivalents of A, L and M. Each is pronounced on its own, as the name of the letter, without a vowel joining it to the next. Because of that the technical term for them is al-muqaṭṭaʿāt, the cut-off or isolated letters. Other surahs open with other combinations, such as Ḥā Mīm, or Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād, or a single letter such as Nūn or Qāf, and some of these combinations have become the names of surahs: Ṭā Hā, Yā Sīn, Ṣād and Qāf. If the repeated letters are removed, the letters used at the openings of surahs come to fourteen, half of the alphabet of twenty-eight: Alif, Lām and Mīm, then Ṣād, Rā and Kāf, then Hā, Yā and ʿAyn, then Ṭā, Sīn and Ḥā, and finally Qāf and Nūn. Glory be to the One who made everything reflect His wisdom, even in so small a detail.

### What the letters mean

The oldest answer is that their meaning is something Allah kept to Himself. Ibn Masʿūd held this, and so did the four caliphs, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī, and it is the view of most of the Companions, of the generation after them, and of the later authorities. Some add that the meaning may have been given to the Prophet ﷺ as a secret he was not to pass on, which would explain why no explanation of the letters has come down from him at all. Al-Qurṭubī adopted this position. He cited ʿĀmir ash-Shaʿbī, Sufyān ath-Thawrī and many masters of hadith for the view that every revealed book contains secret signs of Allah, and that these letters are His secret in the Qur'an. They belong to the elusive verses, the mutashābihāt, whose meaning is known to Allah alone, and it is not for anyone to argue over them. That does not make them useless. Believing in them and reciting them is itself a merit, and in reciting them a person receives blessings from the unseen world whether or not he is aware of it. The four caliphs and Companions such as Ibn Masʿūd held firmly that the letters should be believed in as having come from Allah and recited exactly as they came down, and that it is improper to pry into their meaning.

Other explanations exist beside this one. It was said that the letters are the names of the surahs they begin. It was said that they are the openings Allah chose for His surahs. It was said that they are symbols of His names. Mujāhid said that openings like Alif Lām Rā, Ṭā Sīn Mīm, Ṣād and Qāf are nothing more than letters of the alphabet, and some scholars of language explained that Allah named a few letters and meant the whole alphabet by them, the way a father says "My son recites Alif, Bā, Tā, Thā" and stops there while meaning all twenty-eight. Ibn Jarīr mentioned this opinion. Some held that the letters are an oath that Allah swore.

Ibn ʿAbbās is reported, in the chain that runs through al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ, to have read the three letters as initials: Alif for Allah, Lām for Jibrīl, Mīm for Muhammad ﷺ. Other readings along the same line take Alif as His bounties (ālāʾuh), Lām as His kindness (luṭfuh) and Mīm as His dominion (mulkuh), or as the first letters of three of His names, Allah, al-Laṭīf, the Kind, and al-Majīd, the Glorious. Readings of this sort were given by great and reliable scholars, but their purpose was symbolic. They wanted to wake the reader to the endless meanings that lie in the Qur'an, or to make a difficult thing simple, and none of them claimed that this was what Allah Himself intended. For that reason it is not right to attack such efforts, and it is not right to treat them as the settled meaning either.

### Why the surahs begin with letters

Whatever the letters mean, the scholars agree on what they do. The Qur'an is made of the same letters that the Arabs used in their own speech, yet no one can produce anything like it. Opening surah after surah with bare letters of the alphabet puts that fact on display. This explanation was given by ar-Rāzī in his tafsīr, who traced it to al-Mubarrid and others. Al-Qurṭubī attributed it to al-Farrāʾ and Quṭrub. Az-Zamakhsharī supported it in al-Kashshāf. Abū al-ʿAbbās Ibn Taymiyyah held it, and al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū al-Ḥajjāj al-Mizzī held it too, and he reported that it was the view of Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah. A short gloss puts the same point simply: the letters have no meaning of their own, but they have a purpose, and that purpose is to point to the miracle of a Book built from ordinary letters.

Az-Zamakhsharī explained why the letters are not used once but again and again: repetition makes the challenge bolder, just as the Qur'an repeats its stories and repeats its dare to produce something like it. The openings use one letter, as in Ṣād, Nūn and Qāf, two letters, as in "Ḥâ-Mĩm" (44:1), three, as here, four, as in "Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ra" (13:1) and "Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd" (7:1), and five, as in "Kãf-Ha-Ya-’Aĩn- Ṣãd" (19:1) and "Ḥâ-Mĩm. ’Aĩn-Sĩn-Qãf" (42:1-2). Arabic words are built of one to five letters, so the openings cover every length a word can have.

There is a pattern that supports this reading. Almost every surah that opens with letters goes straight on to speak of the Book itself. Here the letters are followed by "This is the Book! There is no doubt about it" (2:1-2). In Āl ʿImrān they are followed by "He has revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ the Book in truth" (3:1-3). Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād is followed by "˹This is˺ a Book sent down to you" (7:1-2), Alif Lām Rā by "˹This is˺ a Book which We have revealed to you" (14:1), and Alif Lām Mīm in another surah by "The revelation of this Book is—beyond doubt—from the Lord of all worlds" (32:1-2). Ḥā Mīm is followed by "˹This is˺ a revelation from the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful" (41:1-2), and Ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn Qāf by "And so you ˹O Prophet˺ are sent revelation" (42:1-3). The letters, then, come as a kind of signature before the mention of the Book they make up.

### How to hold the question

The scholars said that there is no doubt Allah did not send these letters down as idle play. Some ignorant people claimed that parts of the Qur'an mean nothing, and that is a grave error. The letters carry meaning. If a sound report from the Prophet ﷺ explaining them is found, it is to be accepted. If not, the believer stops where he has been made to stop and says, with those well grounded in knowledge, "We believe in this ˹Quran˺—it is all from our Lord" (3:7). Since the scholars never settled on one explanation, whoever is convinced that one of them is right should follow it, and whoever is not should refrain from judging the matter. Allah knows best what He means by these letters.

### The inner reading

The letters have also been read as the private language of love. Lovers speak to each other in single letters so that no onlooker understands, and between friends there is a secret that words do not disclose and no pen records. Mūsā (Moses) heard a thousand words in a thousand tongues, but this secret was given to Muhammad ﷺ in the seclusion of the night journey, at the distance of "two arms-lengths away or even less" (53:9). Mūsā (Moses) heard the words and did not see the Speaker. Muhammad ﷺ heard the secret while looking upon the One who keeps it. Mūsā (Moses) found his joy in seeking and in hearing, and so much was said to him. Muhammad ﷺ had passed beyond hearing to the point of union, where remembrance is lost in the One remembered and love in the Light, and where a heart that has seen face to face has no more need of reports.

On this reading the three letters are a caress addressed to the best of creation, and they spell out three commands: isolate (afrid) your innermost self for Me, make your limbs supple (layyin) in My service, and stand (aqim) with Me, erasing your own traces and drawing near. The Prophet ﷺ is urged to pass beyond even Jibrīl's mediation so that love may lift the veil and show him the treasures of the unseen, and to drink in one waking moment what the Companions of the Cave drank in a sleep of three hundred and nine years, for the house is empty and the Friend is his. Another reading takes the letters as pronouns: Alif stands for "I" (anā), Lām for "Mine" (lī), Mīm for "from Me" (minnī). I: it is I who am the Lord and who join the servant to Myself in love, the light of the name and of the message, the "serenity" (56:89) of hearts and the rest of spirits. Mine: all that was, is and will be is My kingdom, held by My decree and kept by My protection. From Me: whatever has come has come from My power, My knowledge and My decree. The lesson drawn for the servant is to set aside his own cleverness and knowledge, and to leave the work to his Lord so that he may receive his share.

### In short

- The verse is three isolated letters, read by their names. Twenty-nine surahs open this way, using fourteen different letters in all.
- The four caliphs, Ibn Masʿūd and most scholars held that their meaning is Allah's own secret, to be believed and recited, not probed. Others took them as surah names, as the alphabet in brief, as symbols of His names, or as initials, and such readings were offered as symbols, not as Allah's intended meaning.
- Their purpose is agreed: a Book made of the letters everyone uses, which no one can imitate, and the letters are nearly always followed by mention of the Book.
- The believer accepts what is established, stops where he is made to stop, and says that all of it is from his Lord.

2.text:
After the three letters, the surah makes a claim about the Qur'an itself: "This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺". Three things are said in one breath. This is the Book. It contains no doubt. It guides a particular kind of person. Each phrase carries more than it seems to, and the Companions and the scholars after them drew out of this short verse a whole account of what the Qur'an is, what doubt means, what guidance means, and who the people of taqwā are.

### Phrase by phrase

**"This is the Book!"** In Arabic the pointing word is dhālika, "that", the word used for something at a distance, although the Book is here in front of the reader. The distance is a mark of honour: the demonstrative is used to magnify the Book. There is also a quieter reason. The surah before this one ended with the prayer "Guide us along the Straight Path", and "that Book" points back to the request. The prayer has been answered, and the Qur'an is the answer, the detailed map of the Straight Path for anyone who asks for it and is willing to walk it. The Book is the Qur'an that Muhammad ﷺ was reciting to his people. It has also been said that "the Book" is the Preserved Tablet, or the Book that Allah promised to send down on the day the covenant was taken from the souls, or that the sentence means there is no doubt that the description of Muhammad ﷺ is found in the Torah and the Gospel.

**"There is no doubt about it"** translates lā rayba fīh, and rayb means doubt. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the reports of Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ handed down through as-Suddī, and Ibn Masʿūd with other Companions, in the report of Murrah al-Hamadānī, explained it exactly so: there is nothing in it to doubt. Abū ad-Dardāʾ, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Nāfiʿ, ʿAṭāʾ, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Qatādah and Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid said the same, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim said he knew of no disagreement about it. The meaning is that the Qur'an is beyond doubt revealed from Allah, as the opening of Sūrat as-Sajdah says in almost the same words: "The revelation of this Book is—beyond doubt—from the Lord of all worlds" (32:1-2). Some scholars read the phrase as a command in the form of a statement: do not doubt the Qur'an. There is no doubt about where it came from and no doubt about what it contains. The challenge to anyone who does doubt comes a few verses later: "if you are in doubt about what We have revealed to Our servant, then produce a sûrah like it" (2:23). A thousand people of small or twisted understanding may raise objections, and the sentence remains true.

Where a reciter pauses changes the sense slightly. Some stop after "no doubt" and continue with "in it is guidance for the mindful". It is better to stop after "no doubt about it", because then "a guide" describes the Book itself, which is a stronger statement than saying that guidance can be found inside it. Grammatically, "there is no doubt about it" is what is said about "that Book", and "a guide" is a second statement about it: the Book guides.

**"a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺"** translates hudan lil-muttaqīn. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions said that it means a light for the people of taqwā. The Qur'an is itself guidance, but the guidance in it is received by the righteous in particular. The reason is given in several places: "It is a guide and a healing to the believers. As for those who disbelieve, there is deafness in their ears" (41:44), "We send down the Quran as a healing and mercy for the believers, but it only increases the wrongdoers in loss" (17:82), and "there has come to you a warning from your Lord, a cure for what is in the hearts, a guide, and a mercy for the believers" (10:57). The same light that guides one person leaves another in the dark, and the difference lies in the person.

### Two kinds of guidance

The word hudā is used in the Qur'an for two different things, and both are present in this verse. The first is the faith that lives in the heart. Only Allah can create that, and no one else can put it there, not even a prophet: "You surely cannot guide whoever you like ˹O Prophet˺, but it is Allah Who guides whoever He wills" (28:56), "You are not responsible for people's guidance" (2:272), "Whoever Allah allows to stray, none can guide" (7:186), and "Whoever Allah guides is truly guided. But whoever He leaves to stray, you will never find for them a guiding mentor" (18:17). The second is to explain the truth, point to it and lead toward it. That is what the Prophet ﷺ and the Book do: "you are truly leading ˹all˺ to the Straight Path" (42:52), "You ˹O Prophet˺ are only a warner. And every people had a guide" (13:7), and "As for Thamûd, We showed them guidance, but they preferred blindness over guidance" (41:17). Thamūd were shown the way and refused it. Allah has "shown them the two ways" (90:10), and the correct view is that the two ways are the road of good and the road of evil.

This also answers an obvious objection: surely guidance is needed most by those who are not yet mindful of Allah? The answer lies in degrees. The Qur'an provides guidance to all people, and in one sense to everything in the universe. The first degree of guidance is shared by all mankind and even by animals. The second is particular to human beings and jinn. The third is reserved for those who have drawn near to Allah and found His favour, and that degree has no upper limit. The verse speaks of the last two. For the person who accepts the guidance, there is the hope of rising to the rank of the mindful. For the person who is already mindful, there is more guidance, without end. Specifying the mindful is not a denial of guidance to anyone else.

A further reading makes the same point through human nature. The search for truth is built into a person. Whoever sincerely searches uncovers his own nature, and with Allah's help its vague longings start to receive definite answers. The urge to bow to a higher power becomes bowing to the Almighty. The wish to give oneself for something greater becomes spending one's wealth for Allah's cause. The question about what lies beyond this life finds its answer in faith in the life to come. People who find the truth in this way become free of complexes. They recognise the truth wherever it is and whoever speaks it, and no rigidity, custom or prejudice stands between them and it. Allah protects such people, His order carries them along a sure course in this world, and Paradise is their destination. Only those who seek the truth find it, and whoever seeks it does find it. On this road there is no gap between seeking and finding.

### Who the muttaqīn are

The muttaqīn are the people of taqwā. The word's root meaning is to keep away from what one dislikes, and in the language of the religion it means fearing Allah and keeping away from breaking His commands. Ibn ʿAbbās said the muttaqīn are the believers who keep clear of shirk, associating anything with Allah, and who act in obedience to Him. He also said they are those who fear Allah's punishment, which would fall on them if they left the guidance they recognise and know, and who hope for His mercy by believing in what He revealed. Qatādah said they are the people the next verses describe: those "who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them" (2:3) and what follows. Ibn Jarīr held that the verse includes all of these meanings together, and that is the correct view. Another gloss says they are the people who guard themselves against disbelief, shirk and indecencies, and that the Book is a favour to the believers and a mercy to the mindful of this community. In the shortest description, they lean toward piety by keeping the commands and avoiding what is forbidden, and so shield themselves from the Fire.

ʿAṭiyah as-Saʿdī reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that a servant does not reach the rank of the muttaqīn until he leaves what is harmless for fear of falling into what is harmful. At-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah recorded it, and at-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan gharīb. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb once asked Ubayy ibn Kaʿb what taqwā is. Ubayy asked him whether he had ever walked along a path full of thorns. ʿUmar said he had. "What did you do?" Ubayy asked. ʿUmar said, "I rolled up my sleeves and struggled through." Ubayy said, "That is taqwā."

The verse was also read as Allah speaking directly: this is the Book that has come from Me, and there is no doubt of it. If you believe in it I will guide you, and if you do not, I will punish you.

### The inner reading

"The writing in which there is no doubt" has been taken as an allusion to what Allah has written upon Himself for the community of Muhammad ﷺ, that His mercy outruns His anger, as in "Your Lord has taken upon Himself to be Merciful" (6:54). It has also been taken as the faith and recognition that Allah has written on the hearts of the believers, as in "Allah has instilled faith in their hearts" (58:22). On this reading the verse is a love letter: I have written the mark of faith in your heart, mixed in the perfume of friendship, lit the candle of union, sealed your heart with love and inscribed longing in your awareness. In the Tablet I wrote your description and showed it to Jibrīl. In your heart I wrote My description, and how could I have shown that to an enemy? In the Tablet I wrote your loyalty and your failures. In your heart I wrote praise and recognition, and what I have written about Myself does not change. When Mūsā (Moses) cut a stone from the mountain and the Torah was written on it, the stone turned to emerald. The heart of the one who recognises Allah was hard stone, and when His name was written on it, it became a book of glory. As for "a guide for the godwary", the Qur'an is guidance for the mindful and healing for the faithful, a source of intimacy and a help toward clarity. It is a lamp for hearts and a mirror for the eyes, a key that opens the ears, a cure for pain, light for the eyes of those who know Him, springtime for the spirits of His friends, a warning for the fearful and a mercy for the believers.

### In short

- "That Book" points from afar to honour the Qur'an and points back to the prayer for the Straight Path, which the Qur'an answers.
- There is no doubt about its origin or its contents. The Companions agreed on this meaning without exception, and it is better to pause after "no doubt about it" so that "a guide" describes the Book itself.
- Guidance is of two kinds: the faith only Allah creates in a heart, and the explaining and pointing that the Book and the Prophet ﷺ do. The Qur'an guides everyone in the second sense and the mindful in the first.
- The muttaqīn avoid shirk, obey, fear Allah's punishment and hope for His mercy. Taqwā, in Ubayy's picture, is walking a thorny path with your sleeves rolled up, and in the Prophet's ﷺ words it means leaving the harmless for fear of the harmful.

3.text:
The verse before this one said that the Book guides the mindful. Now the surah says who they are, and it begins with three marks: they are the people "who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them". The first is a matter of the heart, the second of the body, the third of possessions. Together they are a short definition of faith and of the practice that goes with it, and the scholars treated this verse as the place where the Qur'an says, in its own words, what a believer is.

### Phrase by phrase

**"who believe"** translates yuʾminūn, from īmān. ʿAbdullāh, in the report of Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, said that īmān is to trust, and Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, said the same: they trust. Az-Zuhrī said that īmān is the deeds. Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said that "they believe" means they fear Allah. Ibn Jarīr aṭ-Ṭabarī weighed these and preferred to describe the believers as having faith in the unseen with the tongue, with deeds and with conviction. Fear of Allah is then part of the general meaning of īmān, and so is following up what the tongue affirms with action. Īmān, on this account, is a broad word: affirming Allah, His Books and His Messengers, and making that affirmation real by living up to what it implies.

In the language, īmān on its own simply means trust, and the Qur'an sometimes uses it that way. The Prophet ﷺ is described as one who trusts in Allah and trusts the believers (9:61), and the brothers of Yūsuf (Joseph) told their father that he would never believe them even when they spoke the truth (12:17). Sometimes the word is placed beside deeds, as in the exception made for "those who believe and do righteous deeds" (95:6). When īmān is used without restriction, it takes in beliefs, deeds and the statements of the tongue, and it increases and decreases. Some scholars explained īmān as khashyah, fear of Allah, pointing to "those who fear their Lord unseen" (67:12) and to the one "who feared the Most Gracious unseen" (50:33). Fear is the heart of both faith and knowledge, for "it is only those who have knowledge among His servants that fear Allah" (35:28).

A more precise definition looks at how the word is used. In Arabic, īmān means accepting someone's statement with complete certainty because of one's total confidence in him. Confirming something you can see for yourself is not īmān. If one man says a cloth is black and another agrees, that is taṣdīq, confirmation, not faith, because the second man relies on his own eyes and not on the first man's word. In the vocabulary of the Sharīʿah, īmān is accepting with complete certainty what a prophet has said, out of trust in him and without needing to see for oneself. This is worth stressing because "faith" in everyday modern speech has come to mean little more than a strong feeling. Īmān in this sense is a matter of the mind in the old meaning of the word, a settled certainty, not an emotional state.

**"in the unseen"** translates bil-ghayb. The early Muslims explained the ghayb in several ways, all of them correct and all pointing to the same thing. Abū al-ʿĀliyah, in the report of ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, said it means believing in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, the Last Day, His Paradise and His Fire, the meeting with Him, life after death and the Resurrection. Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah said much the same. Another gloss lists what is hidden from people now: Paradise, Hell, the Bridge over Hell, the Scale, the Resurrection and the Reckoning. It has also been said that the unseen is what the Qur'an has revealed of hidden things together with what it has not revealed, and it has even been said that the unseen is Allah Himself.

In the language, ghayb is whatever is not evident to people and cannot be reached by the five senses. The Qur'an uses the word for everything that cannot be known by the senses or by reason alone but has been reported by the Prophet ﷺ: the essence and attributes of Allah, destiny, Paradise and Hell and what is in them, the Day of Judgment and what happens on it, the revealed books and all the prophets before Muhammad ﷺ. In short, everything named in the last two verses of this surah. This verse states the creed in essence, and the last two verses of the surah give its details. So belief in the unseen comes to mean firm faith in everything the Prophet ﷺ taught, provided it has reached us by sound and undeniable transmission, and that is how the great majority of Muslim scholars define īmān in their statements of creed, such as al-ʿAqīdah aṭ-Ṭaḥāwiyyah and the creed of an-Nasafī. On this definition īmān is faith and certainty, not mere knowledge. Satan has knowledge of the truth, and so did many disbelievers, who knew perfectly well that the Prophet ﷺ was truthful and his teaching true, yet had no faith in him and did not accept it with their hearts, and so were not Muslims.

Believing in what one has not seen is the believer's special honour. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Yazīd said that they were sitting with ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and spoke of the Companions and how their deeds were greater than their own. ʿAbdullāh said that the matter of Muhammad ﷺ had been plain to those who saw him, and swore by the One besides whom there is no god that no one would ever attain a better kind of faith than faith in the unseen. Then he recited the opening of this surah, from the letters and "This is the Book" down to the words about those who are successful. Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr recorded this, as did Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Ḥākim in his Mustadrak, who said it is authentic by the standard of al-Bukhārī and Muslim although the two of them did not record it.

A hadith says the same. Ibn Muḥayrīz asked Abū Jumuʿah to narrate something he had heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he told of a meal with the Prophet ﷺ at which Abū ʿUbaydah asked whether anyone was better than they were, who had accepted Islam with him and fought beside him. The Prophet ﷺ said yes: those who would come after them and believe in him without having seen him. Aḥmad recorded it. Abū Bakr ibn Mardawayh recorded another route in his tafsīr, from Ṣāliḥ ibn Jubayr: Abū Jumuʿah al-Anṣārī came to Bayt al-Maqdis, Jerusalem, to pray, and Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah was among those who went out to greet him. As he was leaving he said they had a right over him and a gift coming, and told them that ten of them, Muʿādh ibn Jabal among them, had once asked the Prophet ﷺ whether anyone would earn a greater reward than they had, who believed in Allah and followed him. He answered: what prevents you, when the Messenger of Allah is among you bringing revelation down from heaven? People will come after you who are given a book between two covers, and they will believe in it and act on it. Their reward is greater than yours, even twice as much.

On the inward reading, these are the people who love Allah without having seen Him, who affirm His uniqueness and His oneness in essence and attributes, who hold fast to His Messenger without having seen him and walk straight along his Sunnah. Five hundred years after him, with nothing before them but black ink on white paper, they accept him with spirit and heart. Whatever he reported of the world of the Kingdom, the Lote Tree of the furthest limit, the Gardens of Refuge, the Throne and the end of this world, they testify to and believe in. These are the ones the Prophet ﷺ called his brothers when he said how he longed to meet them.

**"establish prayer"** translates yuqīmūna ṣ-ṣalāh. Ibn ʿAbbās said it means performing the prayer with everything that is obligatory in it, and in the report of aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk he explained it as completing the bowing, the prostration, the recitation, the humility and the attendance at the prayer. Qatādah said it means keeping to its times and to its ablution, bowing and prostration. Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said it means keeping its times, completing one's purification for it, and completing its bowing, prostration, recitation, tashahhud and blessings on the Prophet ﷺ. The verb comes from iqāmah, to set something straight. So the phrase does not mean merely saying one's prayers but performing them correctly in every respect, keeping every condition, whether obligatory (farḍ), necessary (wājib) or recommended (mustaḥabb), and it includes regularity, constancy, inward attention, humility and awe. It is not about one particular prayer. It covers all the farḍ, wājib and nafl prayers, and in the first place the five prescribed prayers with their ablution, their bowing and prostration and their appointed times. In short, the mindful are those who pray regularly and steadfastly according to the rules of the Sharīʿah and keep the inward and outward manners of prayer. In the language, ṣalāh means supplication. In the terminology of the religion it is the act of bowing and prostration with the other specified actions, performed at set times with known conditions and features.

The inward reading describes how they pray: as though they were gazing upon Allah and whispering with Him in private, living out the Prophet's ﷺ words, "Worship Allah as if you see Him, for if you do not see Him, surely He sees you." He also said that when the servant stands for prayer he is before the eyes of the All-Merciful, and when he looks around, Allah says: child of Ādam, at whom are you looking? Are you looking at someone better for you than I? Look at Me, for I am better for you than the one you are looking at. So when you come to prayer, strive to keep your thoughts in it and turn your heart away from the marketplace. Have courtesy, and know the worth of private conversation with the Giver of blessings, for only a person of low aspiration is granted that conversation and then busies his heart with the blessings.

**"and donate from what We have provided for them"** translates wa mimmā razaqnāhum yunfiqūn. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, said it means the zakāh due on their wealth. In the reports of Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, and of Murrah from Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions, it means a man's spending on his family, and this was before zakāh was made obligatory. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said that at first spending in charity was a way of drawing near to Allah at one's own discretion and according to one's means, until the obligation of charity was revealed in the seven verses of Sūrat Barāʾah, which replaced the earlier state of affairs. The position adopted by most commentators is that the phrase includes every form of spending in Allah's way: the obligatory zakāh, the necessary alms and voluntary charity, since the Qur'an generally uses the word infāq for voluntary giving or giving in general and keeps the word zakāh for the obligatory kind. Other glosses say simply that they give in charity from the wealth they have been given, or that they give the zakāh, and it was said that the verse refers to Abū Bakr and his companions. The phrase also teaches by its wording. Everything a person owns is Allah's gift and a trust in his hands, so that giving it all away would be no more than just, and no favour to Him. In His mercy He asks only for spending "from" what He has provided, a part and not the whole.

Allah often names prayer and spending together. Prayer is His right and His worship: it singles Him out for devotion, praises and glorifies Him, calls on Him and shows the servant's dependence on Him. Spending is kindness to His creatures by giving them what benefits them, and those with the first claim on it are relatives, then the wife, then servants, then everyone else. Every kind of required charity and required spending falls under this phrase. Ibn ʿUmar reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Islam is built on five things: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establishing prayer, giving zakāh, fasting Ramaḍān and performing Ḥajj to the House. The two Ṣaḥīḥs record it, and there are many other hadiths to the same effect.

The inward reading adds that the mindful recognise the blessings and favours placed upon them, undertake to be grateful for them, and at the command of the Sharīʿah treat the poor gently, comfort them and regard them as the Real's deputies in receiving charity. That is the road of Muslims in general, who pay what is obligatory or add something voluntarily. The road of the people of inner reality is different: they give away whatever they have and still consider that they have fallen short. Someone asked ash-Shiblī how much zakāh was due on two hundred dirhams. He asked whether the man meant his own or ash-Shiblī's, and when the man said he had not known they were different, he explained: if you give, five dirhams are due, and if I give, the whole two hundred, with five more as a token of thanks. The common people of the community discharge the obligatory zakāh, and the fruit of their work is that they ask, "Lord, are You pleased with what we have given?" The fruit of the deed of the elect, who give everything, is that Allah asks them, "My servant, are you pleased with Me for what you have done?" The two are far apart, and the state of Abū Bakr bears witness to it. After he had given away all he owned, he came one day into the Prophet's ﷺ presence wrapped in a white blanket fastened at the front with a thorn of the date palm. Jibrīl came down with Allah's greeting and the question why Abū Bakr's cloak was pinned with a thorn. The Prophet ﷺ said that he had spent his wealth before the conquest. Jibrīl said that Allah sent him His greetings and asked whether he was content with Him in this poverty of his, or angry. Abū Bakr said, "Should I be angry with my Lord? I am content with my Lord."

It has been said that the servant stands upright through three things, heart, body and possessions. Without faith in the unseen his heart will not go straight in the religion, and neither clarity nor intimacy will appear in him. Without the obligatory prayers his body will not be kept sound and straight with any constancy. And until he separates the zakāh from his possessions, those possessions will not settle down with him.

### Why these three

The two verses that describe the mindful tell the reader who the guided people are and whose path is the Straight Path, so that whoever asks for that path knows whose company to join and whose beliefs and way of life to adopt. That is why, as soon as their qualities are listed, the surah says that they are the ones on guidance from their Lord and the ones who succeed. Of the three qualities named here, faith is the most important, since it is the principle behind every other principle and no good deed is accepted or valid without it. The other two are deeds, and deeds are many. Why only these two? Because every obligatory or necessary good deed concerns either a person's own body or his possessions. Among the acts of worship done with the body the most important is the prayer, so the Qur'an names it. Among those done with possessions, the word infāq covers them all. By naming two deeds the verse has included every form of worship and every good deed, and it describes the mindful as people who are complete in faith and complete in action. It gives a full definition of īmān and, at the same time, the meaning of Islam, since Islam is the sum of faith and practice.

### Īmān and Islam

In the language, īmān means accepting and confirming something in the heart, and Islam means obedience and submission. Īmān belongs to the heart. Islam belongs to the heart too, but also to every other part of the body. In the Sharīʿah, however, neither is valid without the other. Faith in Allah and His Prophet ﷺ in the heart is not enough unless the tongue declares it and submission follows, and a declaration of faith and allegiance on the tongue is not valid without faith in the heart. So the two words differ in their meaning, and the Qur'an and the hadith sometimes speak of the difference, but in the law they are bound together and the Qur'an itself shows that one does not stand without the other.

Where outward submission is not accompanied by inward faith, the Qur'an calls it nifāq, hypocrisy, and treats it as worse than open rejection: "Surely the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of Hell" (4:145). In this world people can judge only what is outward and can never be certain of what is inside a man, so the Sharīʿah requires that those who declare themselves Muslims be treated as Muslims in worldly affairs, while in the next world their fate is worse than that of ordinary disbelievers. Where inward recognition is not accompanied by outward affirmation and allegiance, the Qur'an calls that kufr, denial of the truth. Of the disbelievers it says, "They know him as they know their own sons" (2:146), and of Firʿawn's people, "Their souls knew them to be true, yet they denied them in their wickedness and their pride" (27:14). Sayyid Muhammad Anwar Shāh explained it like this: īmān and Islam cover the same ground in the spiritual journey and differ only in where they begin and end. Īmān starts in the heart and is perfected in outward deeds. Islam starts in outward deeds and is perfected when it reaches the heart. So īmān is not valid if the heart's acknowledgment never reaches outward affirmation, and Islam is not valid if outward affirmation never reaches confirmation by the heart. Al-Ghazzālī and as-Subkī reached the same conclusion, and in his Musāmarah Ibn al-Humām reports that all the reliable scholars agree on it.

A modern note on the same point warns against the confusion that has grown up around these two words under Western influence. Some claim that Islam is only a matter of the "heart" or of "religious experience", and so see no need for fixed ritual or a fixed moral code, treating religion as a purely personal relationship between a person and "his" God. Others insist on nothing but outward performance of rituals or conformity to rules of their own choosing, indifferent to the inward dimension, and some have gone on to replace the rituals Allah ordained with acts of social service dressed up as worship. Others again reduce Islam to a system of social organisation or even to statecraft, so that Muslims who fail to set up a state of a certain shape would cease to be Muslims, which applied to history would mean that no Muslim ever existed. Against all of these, Islam means establishing a relationship of obedience and servitude to Allah. It does not arise from vague experiences or from social regimentation. It requires accepting every doctrine and acting on every command laid down in the Qur'an, the hadith and the Sharīʿah, which cover every sphere of life, from worship to social, political and economic dealings, manners and morals, and whose essential purpose is to produce in a person genuine obedience to Allah. Acting on the Sharīʿah does bring worldly benefits, individual and collective, and those benefits may be called the reason the commands exist, but they are not their essential object, a servant should not obey for their sake, and a Muslim's success as a Muslim does not depend on obtaining them. When a person has fully submitted to Allah's commands in all he does, he has already succeeded as a Muslim, whether or not the worldly benefits follow.

The same three qualities can be seen as the growth of a seeker. The urge to make out the world of meanings behind the world of forms, when it leads to discovery, becomes faith in the unseen. The urge to submit to a higher power becomes bowing to the Almighty. The wish to give oneself for something greater becomes spending one's wealth in Allah's cause.

### In short

- Īmān is accepting with certainty what the Prophet ﷺ reported, out of trust in him and without seeing for oneself. It lives in the heart, is spoken by the tongue, is proved by deeds, and it increases and decreases.
- The unseen is everything beyond the senses that revelation reports: Allah and His attributes, the angels, the Books, the Messengers, destiny, death and Resurrection, the Reckoning, Paradise and Hell. Believing without seeing is a higher faith than the Companions' own, by Ibn Masʿūd's oath and by the Prophet's ﷺ words about those who would come after.
- Establishing prayer means praying on time, in purity, with complete bowing, prostration, recitation and humility, and keeping it up for life.
- Spending from what Allah provides covers zakāh, required support and voluntary charity, and it asks for a part, not the whole, of what is in any case His gift and His trust.
- Faith, prayer and spending stand for heart, body and possessions, so the verse defines the whole of Islam, which is faith and practice together, neither valid without the other.
